b: In this episode, Peter welcomes back Jeff Cavaliere, a physical therapist, strength coach, and founder of ATHLEAN-X who has spent decades bridging the gap between rehabilitation, athletic performance, and strength training. Jeff begins by sharing how his experience working with professional athletes and managing his own injuries has shaped his approach to building strength and muscle while minimizing injury risk. He discusses how training should evolve as we age, particularly for those in their 40s, 50s, and beyond who want to continue making progress without compromising long-term joint health. Jeff explains why excessive training volume can be counterproductive and how to balance reps in reserve with training to failure to maximize results while managing fatigue and injury risk. He also explores the differences between training for aesthetics and functional performance, explaining why these goals are not necessarily at odds. The conversation then shifts to a muscle-by-muscle breakdown of effective exercises for building strength and hypertrophy. Jeff highlights common training mistakes, offers modifications for those dealing with pain or injury, and explains why often-neglected muscles deserve more attention. Finally, he walks through his “exercise graveyard,” identifying popular exercises that may carry unnecessary injury risk and offering alternatives that deliver similar benefits with less risk. Throughout the episode, Jeff provides actionable guidance for making training more effective, sustainable, and adaptable as we age.

Jeff’s passion as an educator and the path that led him to build his YouTube channel [2:30, V: 0:11];
Briefly tell us a little bit about your journey and how you found your way to doing what you’re doing right now
Some people may not know a lot about you, and we didn’t talk about it in the roundtable
⇒ Jeff was a guest in the roundtable episode on strength training, #365
Growing up, Jeff always wanted to get involved in a career where he could help or educate people

His father was a doctor, and he had aspirations at one point to become a doctor, because no one of his siblings had
He was the third kid of three
If he could figure out a way he could work with athletes at the same time as helping people, that would be his perfect fit

He started working strictly with athletes when he got a job with the New York Mets as a physical therapist
He was their head physical therapist for 3 seasons, and he also served as their strength coach
Then he left to pursue what he ultimately became

He started pretty early making educational videos for YouTube
Focusing on taking the lessons he learned from training top-level athletes and applying them to people who were never going to get paid to do this
To people who just wanted to be able to benefit from what they needed to focus on to perform at such a high level
“Because I think we all have a lot more we can do if we focus on the right things.”‒ Jeff Cavaliere
Jeff started off with a couple videos and the next thing you knew, a couple more subscribers
He saw that there was an opportunity to continue to pursue that path
And ultimately, now he has almost 15 million subscribers

He’s doing what he’s done since day one, which is just trying to use the platform to educate and empower people with the techniques and strategies from the realms of rehab as a physical therapist and strength and conditioning
To him, rehab and strength and conditioning are all one continuum
If you’re hurt, you’re just less functional at the moment
But as you become able to get higher and higher levels of function, you could get to extreme levels of function and capabilities and that’s athleticism
What year did you start your YouTube channel in earnest?
2009 is when he actually started making content for it
His years with the Mets was 2006, ‘07, and ‘08
Peter points out that there’s so much content on there
When you think about the evolution of the channel, how do you think about that from the standpoint of injury prevention?
Peter has been following Jeff for a while ‒ he discovered him on Instagram a few years ago

Peter noticed his discussion on doing a lat pulldown: you’re not getting the right engagement
This is geared toward function and hypertrophy
This is not about an injury
This is about making progress
Has that been an evolution for you or have you always provided information on that continuum?
Jeff has always provided people information on that continuum because he feels that’s the part where his skill as a physical therapist comes in

Because if you’re in a rehab setting, and somebody comes to you with whatever ailment they have at the moment, and they need help, you will never be able to follow the playbook as instructor or as written or as the protocol comes that says, “This is what you’re doing one week later, two weeks later, three weeks post-op, whatever.”

Something always comes up where that individual has something that doesn’t feel right, or they don’t have the range of motion that’s expected, or something is preventing the playbook from being able to be executed
That’s where you need to be flexible enough to be able to say, “Well, okay, try this instead.”
It could just be simply moving your leg further out into abduction to then go do a leg lift ‒ all of a sudden, pain-free motion (and they’re able to do the activity again)
If you don’t have that ability to have a lot of flexibility in your approach, then you can’t effectively perform a rehab on somebody
It’s no different in weight training and strength training
Not every exercise will feel great for every person or feel as effective as it should

There’s tips that you can give them to increase the stimulus that you’re feeling, and that might work for almost everybody, but there’s still going to be people who don’t have that effect with the exercise they’re doing
So you need to find exercise #2 or #3
“The beautiful thing about strength and conditioning is there’s never just one option. There’s usually hundreds of options to go to.”‒ Jeff Cavaliere
So if you’re diverse in your playbook, you’re going to be able to do that
Over the years, Jeff’s ability to navigate similar issues has grown
He’s done 1,700 videos at this point

He’s covered a lot of the same issues twice
But coming at it from a different angle
And making it click for somebody for the first time because he’s explaining it slightly differently (that’s where the power is)
Are you still making a lot of long-form content?
Peter thinks Jeff has probably observed the same thing that many people have observed, which is some combination of the human attention span appears to be getting shorter and shorter
And platforms seem to recognize that and prioritize shorter and shorter content

Peter thinks he’s a bit of an unusual person in that he doesn’t like short-form content
He really likes long-form content
He likes watching a 20-minute video where he will learn something in depth that’s at the master’s level
As opposed to a one-minute video that just shows me something at a superficial level that, obviously, even if it’s correct, it’s incomplete
How has your ability to provide content evolved in that environment?

It’s been a huge challenge for Jeff personally
Because like Peter, he likes to find that long-form content, dive deep

He has no problem taking a 3-hour podcast or even a 40-minute video and chunking it down into sessions
So that he can watch 10 minutes now and then 10 minutes later

What he doesn’t like is the watering down or the thinning out of the content
Specifically because it needs to fit this short-form format

In the short-form format, what you’re forced to do as an educator is to pick and choose the things that you think are going to be the most impactful, but you’re not really even given the opportunity to explain why
Jeff makes the point, “I’ll give you a great soundbite, but is the soundbite really valuable if you don’t also understand why?”
Because unless you remember or memorize that soundbite and can implement whatever the soundbite’s telling you to do
If you forget the why, then you may never be able to actually understand why you’re doing what you were told
That is why Jeff has always done long-form content because he wants to have the opportunity to explain
Jeff shares, “We have a joke internally at my company where they say, ‘Sets and reps, please,’ because that’s what people literally will say in comments.”
They’ll bypass the entire explanation of why
Again, Jeff is not trying to make a long video

He’s trying to give you the information that you need to be able to implement this
Not just on whatever I’m teaching you in that video, but other things too
“Sets and reps, please,” is basically the punchline to like, “I don’t want to hear any of that. I just want to know—tell me the what.”
Jeff still struggles, but he will always continue to make long-form content
Now he’s had to make short-form content
He’s had to take clips from these longer videos and convert them into things he can present in short-form format

He had to make the more intentionally engaging in the first 3 seconds because he knows that is the attention span of the person who’s about ready to flip that thumb one more time and skip right past him
Jeff wants to catch their eye just so he can have the opportunity to teach them whatever he thinks is going to be valuable
He thinks that’s that a game that kind of sucks, but it’s part of what social media is evolving into
Peter thinks the good news is that we’re 10 minutes into this discussion, and any of the people that need to get hooked in the first 3 seconds are not only gone, they’re 10 steps removed
Anybody who’s still sticking around is in this for the long haul, so we should not be apologetic for the fact that we’re going to talk about many topics in depth
